text:
Person class


Data

first name
last name
age

Operations

__init__
__str__
fullname
email






Build methods for Person


Edit the code, then click Run.




Run


Reset



class Person:
    def __init__(self, first, last, age):
        self.first = first
        self.last = last
        self.age = age

    def fullname(self):
        return f"{self.first} {self.last}"

    def email(self):
        return f"{self.first.lower()}.{self.last.lower()}@uvu.edu"

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.fullname()} ({self.age})"

p = Person("Harry", "Potter", 17)
print(p)
print(p.fullname())
print(p.email())

title: Introduction to Classes and Objects
text:
PersonList


Data
A list that stores Person objects.
Operations

add(self, person_obj)
__str__(self)






Store Person objects in a list


Students can modify the list contents and rerun the example.




Run


Reset



class Person:
    def __init__(self, first, last, age):
        self.first = first
        self.last = last
        self.age = age

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.first} {self.last} ({self.age})"

class PersonList:
    def __init__(self):
        self.people = []

    def add(self, person_obj):
        self.people.append(person_obj)

    def __str__(self):
        return "\n".join(str(p) for p in self.people)

group = PersonList()
group.add(Person("Hope", "Smith", 20))
group.add(Person("Jack", "Jones", 19))
print(group)

Output

title: Introduction to Classes and Objects
text:
Shallow Copy vs Deep Copy

A shallow copy copies the object, but nested mutable attributes may still be shared.
A deep copy copies the object and nested objects too.

title: Introduction to Classes and Objects
section: Interactive: Shallow Copy vs Deep Copy
text:
Interactive: Shallow Copy vs Deep Copy




Run the copy example


Try changing which object is mutated, or add id(…) to compare identities.




Run


Reset



from copy import copy, deepcopy

class Person:
    def __init__(self, first, last, age, courses=None):
        self.first = first
        self.last = last
        self.age = age
        self.courses = [] if courses is None else courses

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.first} {self.last}: {self.courses}"

p1 = Person("Hope", "Smith", 2, ["CS1410", "CS2420"])

p2 = p1
p3 = copy(p1)
p4 = deepcopy(p1)

p2.first = "Jack"
p3.courses[0] = "CS1400"
p4.courses[0] = "CS1030"

print("p1:", p1)
print("p2:", p2)
print("p3:", p3)
print("p4:", p4)

Output

title: Introduction to Classes and Objects
text:
Some Object-Oriented Terms

Class: a type; an abstraction of related objects
Instance/Object: a unique object containing its own data
Attribute: a data element inside an instance
Method: a function that operates on an instance
Interface: the collection of methods defined by a class
State: the current values in the attributes of an instance
Instantiation: creating an object from a class

title: Introduction to Classes and Objects
text:
The Interface of Student class







Method
What It Does




Student(name, number)
Creates a Student object with the given name and number of scores. Each score is initially 0.


get_name()
Returns the student’s name


get_score(i)
Returns the student’s ith score


set_score(i, score)
Resets the student’s ith score


get_average()
Returns the student’s average score


get_high_score()
Returns the student’s highest score


__str__()
Returns a string representation of the student’s information

Method Definitions

Method definitions are indented under the class statement.
The syntax is like a regular function.
Each instance method includes a first parameter for the object itself.
Conventionally, that parameter is named self.

title: Introduction to Classes and Objects
text:
Example Method: get_score()




Use an accessor method




Run


Reset



class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, nscores):
        self.name = name
        self.scores = [0] * nscores

    def get_score(self, i):
        assert 1 <= i <= len(self.scores)
        return self.scores[i - 1]

    def set_score(self, i, score):
        assert 1 <= i <= len(self.scores)
        self.scores[i - 1] = score

s = Student("Luna", 5)
s.set_score(4, 88)
print(s.get_score(4))

title: Introduction to Classes and Objects
text:
The __str__ Magic Method

Classes often include an __str__ method.
It builds and returns a string representation of an object’s state.
When str(obj) or print(obj) is used, __str__ is called automatically.
This is especially useful for debugging.

title: Introduction to Classes and Objects
text:
Student __str__




Write a string representation




Run


Reset



class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, nscores):
        self.name = name
        self.scores = [0] * nscores

    def __str__(self):
        str_score = [str(s) for s in self.scores]
        str_score = " ".join(str_score)
        return f"Name: {self.name}\nScores: {str_score}"

s = Student("Maria", 5)
s.scores[0] = 95
s.scores[1] = 82
print(s)

Output

title: Introduction to Classes and Objects
text:
Accessors and Mutators


Accessor
Reads a value but does not change it.
Mutator
Changes a value.





Try get_score and set_score




Run


Reset



class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, nscores):
        self.name = name
        self.scores = [0] * nscores

    def get_score(self, i):
        assert 1 <= i <= len(self.scores)
        return self.scores[i - 1]

    def set_score(self, i, score):
        assert 1 <= i <= len(self.scores)
        self.scores[i - 1] = score

s = Student("Kai", 3)
print("before:", s.scores)
s.set_score(2, 77)
print("after:", s.scores)
print("score 2 =", s.get_score(2))

Output

title: Introduction to Classes and Objects
text:
Class Variables and Methods

Class variables belong to the class, not each object.
All instances share the same class variable.
Class methods receive cls, not self.
They can be called from the class or from an instance.
Class methods can be used as alternative constructors.





Run a class variable example




Run


Reset



class Student:
    SCHOOL = "UVU"

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

s1 = Student("Harry")
s2 = Student("Maria")

print("Before change:")
print(s1.name, Student.SCHOOL)
print(s2.name, Student.SCHOOL)

Student.SCHOOL = "Westminster"

print("\nAfter change:")
print(s1.name, Student.SCHOOL)
print(s2.name, Student.SCHOOL)

Output

title: Introduction to Classes and Objects
text:
Class methods

Use the @classmethod decorator.
Take cls as the special parameter.
Have access to the class, but not a particular object instance.





Use @classmethod as an alternative constructor




Run


Reset



class Student:
    SCHOOL = "UVU"

    def __init__(self, name, year):
        self.name = name
        self.year = year

    @classmethod
    def freshman(cls, name):
        return cls(name, 1)

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.name}, year {self.year}, school {self.SCHOOL}"

s = Student.freshman("Avery")
print(s)

Output

text:
__new__ vs. __init__


__new__: Constructor

Creates and returns a new object.
Runs before __init__.
Usually inherited from object.


__init__: Initializer

Initializes an object after it has been created.
Receives the new object as self.
Usually sets instance variables and initial state.


Order: __new__ creates the object → __init__ initializes the object.




Run the order of execution




Run


Reset



class Person:
    def __new__(cls, *args, **kwargs):
        print("__new__: create the object")
        obj = super().__new__(cls)
        return obj

    def __init__(self, name):
        print("__init__: initialize the object")
        self.name = name

p = Person("Harry")
print("name =", p.name)

Output

Class Models… Method Models…


Class models…
A thing. A kind of thing. A type of thing. Attributes of a thing.
In a problem description, look for nouns.

Method models…
An action. An operation. An algorithm. Behavior of a thing.
In a problem description, look for verbs.

Develop a short list of methods available to users.
Write a short snippet that uses the new class.
These “use cases” can also be represented in UML.
